Tier1Alpha: the concern with Intel $INTC is that the impact [of today's drop] could extend well beyond its direct index weighting, given its much larger concentration in the semiconductor complex and the additional selling pressure that could come from [leveraged ETF such as $SOXL] rebalancing....

While INTC holds only a 0.70% weighting in SPX, it is currently the second-largest holding in [the Philadelphia Semiconductor ETF] SOXX at about 8.3%, meaning a decline of this magnitude is likely to drag down the broader semiconductor index and could create a significant MOC imbalance in SOXL, its 3x leveraged equivalent. This matters even more because SOXL is back over $25B in AUM, meaning there's more notional to hedge per point of volatility....

Since SOXL tracks the broader semiconductor index with roughly 30 other stocks...hedging flows can potentially drive higher correlation among other constituents in the index, even if those names have little direct exposure to Intel's earnings. And, as mentioned above, given how significant semiconductor stocks have become to both SPX and NDX, there is a much higher chance of a broader spillover effect, as single-stock risk transmits into sector risk, and eventually broader index risk.

[Note the $SOXX ETF is currently lower by 6.6% in the pre-market an ~2.7 standard deviation move which would result in over $10B in notional selling in SOX]

The Employment Cost Index (#ECI), the Fed’s favorite wage gauge, rose 0.79% quarter-over-quarter, in line with expectations for 0.8% and the least since Q4 2025. Year-over-year it eased to 3.37%, the least since Q2 2021, down from a 5.1% peak in 2022, and adjusted for inflation, compensation fell 0.4% year-over-year, the weakest since Q4 2022, versus a 0.5-0.6% 1990-2019 average

▪️ Wages and salaries: +0.7% quarter-over-quarter, 3.1% year-over-year, the least since Q1 2021
▪️ Benefits: +0.9% quarter-over-quarter, 3.9% year-over-year, the most since Q3 2023 (private health benefits +6.4%)
▪️ Leisure and hospitality wages: 2.2%, the least since Q1 2016
▪️ Goods-producing wages: 3.1%, the least since Q1 2021
▪️ Union wages 4.3% vs. nonunion 3.0%

While nominal pay growth is still above anything seen in 2010-2019, when it peaked at 3.0% in Q4 2018, with  CPI up 3.7% over the year, real compensation is shrinking, and the softest pay growth is in lower-wage service jobs.  

In another trend, benefits have outpaced wages for four straight quarters. 

Overall the report fits the September FOMC minutes, where some officials said the labor market was “not currently a source of inflationary pressures.”

Goldman: Because no single survey question identifies whether AI caused a given job loss, we construct a composite score capturing the likelihood that it did, drawing on the occupation and industry in which the job was lost and the stated reason for separation. 

The score rises with the occupation's exposure to AI and the industry's AI adoption rate and is higher when the job loss reflected the elimination of a position. 

We find that, since 2025, workers most likely displaced by AI—those in the top 30% of our score—have faced more difficult transitions back into employment than other displaced workers. As Exhibit 1 shows, they took about a month longer to find a new job and were roughly 10pp more likely to remain unemployed a year after displacement.

GDPNow Tracking Slowdown in Q4

Consistent with my note yesterday morning, Q3 GDP came in at 3.37%, just 0.10 pt above the Atlanta Fed GDPNow’s final 3.27% nowcast, fitting both of the tendencies I (or I guess I should say Claude) flagged: 

1 - after a big drop in the final month, and 
2 - in third quarters, 

the actual print has usually come in close to but above GDPNow’s last read.

GDPNow has now landed within about a tenth of the actual print in 5 of the last 9 quarters.

Turning to Q4, the Atlanta Fed has now started tracking at 3.22%:

▪ Consumption +1.79 pts (vs +2.55 in the final Q3 nowcast)
▪ Business spending +1.22 (vs +1.73)
▪ Inventories +0.59 (vs +1.64)
▪ Government +0.21 (vs +0.44)
▪ Residential −0.18 (vs −0.13)
▪ Net exports −0.41 (vs −2.95)

My usual caveat: GDPNow’s early nowcasts of a quarter have historically run high. It has started above the advance print in 34 of 57 quarters (ex-2020), by 0.40 pt on average. All three 2026 openings ended well lower:
▪ Q1: 3.13% → 1.99%
▪ Q2: 3.70% → 1.50%
GDPNow Tracking Slowdown in Q4 Q3: 4.95% → 3.37%

Several posts in @C_Barraud’s morning brief flagged the return of Europe’s gas squeeze, a situation in large part of the continent’s own making.

Dutch TTF futures broke €100/MWh Wednesday for the first time since December 2022 (Bloomberg), more than triple the pre-Iran-war level. That leaves the EU in an uncomfortable spot after it failed to take advantage of a dip in prices this spring.

EU storage exited last winter at ~28% in early April vs. 35% a year earlier (European Gas Hub). Yet even as TTF fell to about $15/MMBtu (~€45/MWh) after the April 8 U.S.-Iran ceasefire, refilling lagged. The seasonal curve was inverted (winter contracts priced below summer), so expectations were for cheaper future prices, and the EU has no common mechanism to force injections. Spring injections ran ~20% below 2025.

Exacerbating matters, Brussels had loosened the rules in 2025, letting states fall up to 10 points short of the 90% winter start storage target under “difficult conditions” such as low seasonal spreads or high prices.

The result: EU storage is 74.6% full, ~15 points below the five-year average (Gas Infrastructure Europe). Equinor’s CEO says that’s the lowest for this time of year since 2011.

Adding to the pressure, a “Dunkelflaute” (a cold, windless, cloudy spell) is expected to keep German wind generation below 7 GW through next week, less than half this year’s average (Bloomberg).

The upshot? German day-ahead power for Thursday cleared above €300/MWh, about double October’s average (Epex Spot via Bloomberg). It was €13 on Sunday.

Energy Aspects warns TTF could top €200 if the winter turns cold and supplies stay tight, vs. a U.S. equivalent near €8.5. Europe let the forward curve, not policy, decide whether to refill, and now it’s bidding against Asia for spot LNG at more than twice the spring price.
